name: QEMU linux-user aarch64: -R accepts up to MAX_RESERVED_VA = (1<<52)-1 because TARGET_VIRT_ADDR_SPACE_BITS is 52, so a 4 PiB reservation passes QEMU's own bound check
component: qemu-aarch64 linux-user: handle_arg_reserved_va + pgb_addr_set (aarch64 does not override MAX_RESERVED_VA)
required_postconditions: one contiguous PROT_NONE range of 2^52 bytes exists at guest_base
reserved_va <= MAX_RESERVED_VA(cpu) == (1ul << 52) - 1 is QEMU's only compiled-in ceiling; the host's own ceiling is not consulted

failure_sink.description: main.c:839 only rejects reserved_va > max_reserved_va, and max_reserved_va is (1<<52)-1 for aarch64, so -R 4P survives argument validation. The failure surfaces later as 'Unable to find a guest_base to satisfy all guest address mapping requirements' + exit(EXIT_FAILURE).

source_locations.symbol: if (max_reserved_va && reserved_va > max_reserved_va) -> 'Reserved virtual address too big' + exit
#define MAX_RESERVED_VA arm_max_reserved_va - 32-bit ARM overrides the ceiling to 0xffffffff; aarch64 has no such override, so the generic 2^52 formula applies

extraction_limitations: the 2^52 size is the maximum the code accepts, not a value QEMU picks by default: for a 64-bit target on a 64-bit host reserved_va stays 0 unless the user passes -R. This document models the -R 4P invocation.
the size given is 2^52 exactly; QEMU stores reserved_va as size-1 (main.c:403), so the actual reservation is [0, 2^52-1].

x_campaign.quote:
#   define MAX_RESERVED_VA(CPU)  ((1ul << TARGET_VIRT_ADDR_SPACE_BITS) - 1)
---
#ifdef TARGET_AARCH64
# define TARGET_VIRT_ADDR_SPACE_BITS  52
x_campaign.rationale: x86-64 Linux gives a user process at most 47 bits of address space (probe measured max_user_address 0x7ffffffff000); a 2^52-byte contiguous reservation is 32x larger than the entire address space and can never succeed.
x_campaign.note_after_schema_fix: QEMU maps over its PROT_NONE reservation and checks THAT call; it is not the Windows two-phase model.
